label: Hats and accessories
rationale: The rest of what you wear, each with its own verb: a hat is pulled on with kaburu, a ring and a tie just take suru, perfume goes on with tsukeru.
mixUps: kaburu for anything over the head, suru for small worn items (as in masuku o suru), tsukeru for things put onto the body; a hat comes off with toru or nugu, a ring or tie with hazusu.

targets.verbSense: pull over or put on the head
targets.trap: Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.
targets.use: Usually boushi kabutteru (has a hat on) or boushi kabutte (put your hat on). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Off: boushi o toru or nugu. kaburu also means 'clash', as in yotei ga kaburu.

example.ja: 今日帽子かぶってるね。
example.english: Oh, you've got a hat on today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa boushi o kabuttemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は帽子をかぶってますね。

targets.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
targets.trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: a ring, like a watch, mask or tie, takes suru (yubiwa shiteru).
targets.use: Mostly heard as yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on) or shitenai, very often about a wedding ring: kekkon yubiwa shiteru. Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Slipping one on is often yubiwa o hameru, the same verb as for gloves (tebukuro o hameru), and hameteru also means has one on; yubiwa o tsukeru is fine too, a little more formal. The finger takes ni: kusuriyubi ni yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on the ring finger). It comes off with hazusu.

example.romaji: ano hito, kekkon yubiwa shiteru ne.
example.ja: あの人、結婚指輪してるね。
example.english: Oh, he's wearing a wedding ring.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa kekkon yubiwa o shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は結婚指輪をしてますね。

targets.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
targets.trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie takes suru, like a mask or a watch (nekutai shiteru). nekutai o shimeru is tying it, and shimeteru is also a slightly more formal 'has one on'. It comes off with hazusu or toru.
targets.use: Mostly heard as nekutai shiteru (has a tie on) or, in dress-code talk, nekutai shinakute ii (no tie needed). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Loosening it is nekutai o yurumeru; the summer kuuru bizu dress code means noo nekutai (no tie).

example.romaji: kyou wa nekutai shinakute ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はネクタイしなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't need a tie today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nekutai o shinakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はネクタイをしなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to wear a tie today.

targets.verbSense: attach, apply; put on (jewellery, perfume, cream)
targets.trap: Not kousui o kiru: perfume takes tsukeru, the verb for anything applied or attached (earrings, a necklace, cream). kiru is only for clothes on the torso or whole body.
targets.use: Heard as kousui tsuketeru? (are you wearing perfume?) or as a complaint, tsukesugi (too much). Casual speech drops o. tsuketeru means it's on, not that someone is putting it on now.
targets.notes: For spraying it on, kousui o kakeru is also common (12 corpus hits against 19 for tsukeru).

example.ja: いい匂い、香水つけてる？
example.english: You smell nice, are you wearing perfume?

examplePolite.romaji: ii kaori desu ne. kousui o tsuketeru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いい香りですね。香水をつけてるんですか？
examplePolite.english: What a lovely scent. Are you wearing perfume?
